author: Michael McCarthy, Jeanne McCarten & Helen Sandiford
introFa: کتاب «Viewpoint 2» نوشته Michael McCarthy, Jeanne McCarten & Helen Sandiford یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Viewpoint 2»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Commentaries on Viewpoint: The rigorous study of exercise adaptations: Why mRNA might not be enough COMMENTARY ON VIEWPOINT: THE RIGOROUS STUDY OF EXERCISE ADAPTATIONS: WHY mRNA MIGHT NOT BE ENOUGH TO THE EDITOR: Miller and colleagues (1) argue that mRNA should be used as a supportive rather than primary outcome in exercise-training studies. In general, this is a highly valid position because far too many studies have made conclusions that are based on the assumption that a change in mRNA means a change at the protein level. However, in some studies, measuring mRNA as a primary outcome is perfectly accept- able. For instance, if the goal of a study is to deﬁne the mechanisms through which exercise controls the expression of a speciﬁc gene (e.g., a promoter bashing study), then measur- ing mRNA as the primary outcome would be highly appropri- ate. Miller and colleagues also stated that including assess- ments of posttranscriptional regulation would enhance the scientiﬁc rigor of exercise studies. Again, there is a great deal of validity to their argument; yet the same argument could be made for the need to assess posttranslational modiﬁcations and ultimately the biological/functional signiﬁcance of the changes being reported. At the end of the day, the goals of every study are unique, and there are limitations to what can/should be measured within a single study. Therefore, I believe that we should avoid the restrictions of a mindset that dictates that certain types of measurements are, or are not, scientiﬁcally rigorous enough for exercise-training studies. Instead, I think that we as authors, and peer reviewers, simply need to be more critical when evaluating whether the conclusions of a study are supported by scientiﬁcally rigorous data. REFERENCE 1. Miller BF, Konopka AR, Hamilton KL. Viewpoint: The rigorous study of exercise adaptations: why mRNA might not be enough. J Appl Physiol; doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00137.2016. Troy A. Hornberger University of Wisconsin-Madison BEYOND mRNA: EXERCISE ADAPTATIONS REQUIRE REGULATION AT MULTIPLE STEPS WITHIN THE GENE EXPRESSION PATHWAY TO THE EDITOR: We appreciate the authors’ Viewpoint (4) regarding the use of mRNA alone as an outcome measure for exercise training studies. Our view, consistent with theirs, is that the adaptations to exercise consist of time- dependent alterations in molecular events initiated by sig- naling created by acute exercise (2). These include changes in mRNA levels, which are determined by transcription as well as degradation rates due to mRNA stability factors. We do believe that there is a place for mRNA measurements in exercise studies: 1) mRNA levels are an acute reﬂection of signaling affecting transcription or mRNA stability; 2) gene chip technology has made it possible to measure thousands of transcripts simultaneously, presenting an unbiased search opportunity that can lead to unexplored signaling paths; 3) when combined with protein measures, mRNA levels can provide insight into the regulation of gene expression. We consider gene expression as a “pathway” subject to multiple levels of control. In the area of exercise and mitochondrial biogenesis, mRNA levels represent one step among gene transcription, mRNA stability, translation, protein import into mitochondria and assembly into holoenzymes (1, 3). Indeed, we contend that a component of posttranscriptional regulation that is understudied in the exercise literature is protein trafﬁcking. The translocation of proteins to the nucleus to regulate transcription, the transport of cargo to the lysosome for degradation, and the import of proteins into mitochondria are examples of this, the investigation of which would enhance the thoroughness of studies seeking to understand the molecular adaptations of muscle to exercise. Carter David A. Hood York University COMMENTARY ON VIEWPOINT: THE RIGOROUS STUDY OF EXERCISE ADAPTATIONS: WHY mRNA MIGHT NOT BE ENOUGH TO THE EDITOR: In general, we agree with Miller et al. (3) on the limitations of using mRNA expression as a primary outcome measurement in exercise studies. We suggest that incorporation of 5-ethynyl uridine (EU) to label newly transcribed RNA will signiﬁcantly enhance the value of RNA measurements by allowing one to determine if changes in mRNA levels are the result of transcription and/or mRNA stability (2). A related point that we consider to be equally problematic is the common use of measuring mRNA expression derived from whole muscle as a speciﬁc readout of satellite cell activity. This practice is extremely limited because the vast majority (93–97%) of nuclei in muscle are myonuclei, which means the contribution of satellite cell derived mRNA to the total RNA pool is exceedingly minor (5). Using EU-labeling, we recently reported that the predomi- nant source of newly synthesized RNA at rest and after mechanical overload is myonuclei not satellite cells (2). There is an underlying assumption that changes in the expression of myogenic regulatory factors or cell cycle regulators derived from whole muscle homogenate is indic- ative of satellite cell activity. This assumption is seriously J Appl Physiol 121: 597–600, 2016; doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00509.2016. McCarthy University of Kentucky NO TIME LIKE THE RIGHT mRNA TIME TO THE EDITOR: The molecular bases of skeletal muscle adapta- tion to exercise involves increased expression and/or activity of key proteins, mediated by an array of signaling events, pre- and posttranscriptional processes, regulation of translation and pro- tein expression, and modulation of protein (enzyme) activities and/or intracellular localization (2). These responses are tran- sient, extremely variable between individuals, and subject to multiple regulatory points (1). The Viewpoint by Miller and colleagues (3) highlights the limitations of using any single outcome measure in this integrated sequence of events to explain exercise adaptation. Adaptations to exercise training result from the cumula- tive effect of transient increases in mRNA transcripts that encode for various proteins after each successive exercise bout (4). Yet despite numerous studies that have reported postexercise mRNA responses, a comprehensive analyses of the time course of the molecular events underlying exercise response-adaptations is lacking. Part of the reason for this gap in our knowledge is that is it unreasonable to expect healthy individuals to undergo the multiple biopsies re- quired to obtain the detailed time course of exercise-induced responses. Indeed, biopsy sampling time points in published investigations have, unwittingly, framed our current “under- standing” of the impact of exercise on molecular (mRNA) responses. This information has, in turn, impacted our interpretation of published data sets and shaped subsequent experimental design. Future studies should provide detailed analyses of the time course of exercise-induced regulatory events, a task made difﬁcult because of the multitude of factors that inﬂuence such responses (e.g., exercise modal- ity, training history, ﬁber type, sex, and energy status). Hawley Australian Catholic University, Liverpool John Moores University INTEGRATIVE BIOLOGY IS NEEDED TO UNDERSTAND EXERCISE ADAPTATIONS FROM THE WHOLE BODY TO THE CELLULAR LEVEL TO THE EDITOR: In a recent Viewpoint, Miller et al. (2) argued that determining mRNA levels is not sufﬁcient to understand the molecular mechanisms of physical exercise (PE)-induced health beneﬁts. High-throughput techniques have been exten- sively used in the last decade to determine the transcriptome signature in response to PE (1). Although changes in mRNA levels are indicative of signaling events and molecular adap- tations to PE, we agree that this approach is limited and should only be used as one tool alongside others to understand the mechanisms underlying exercise adaptations. Adaptations to PE are often only investigated in skeletal muscle and the cardiorespiratory system. However, PE perturbs whole body homeostasis and involves a myriad of adaptive responses, including a hierarchical and coordinated control across multi- ple organ systems, tissues, cells, and subcellular compartments (3). Furthermore, growing evidence indicates that autocrine, paracrine, and endocrine factors are released to modulate physiological responses within and across tissues during PE (5). In addition to this spatial control, PE inﬂuences the temporal control of circadian rhythms and molecular clocks, which may have a role in improving human health (4). The future challenge will be to use an integrative approach to deﬁne the response to PE. The advent of “omics” technologies, including genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics creates new possibilities for deﬁning the molecular responses to PE (3). The application of large-scale unbiased “omics” platforms combined with bioinformatics analyses will allow us to understand multilevel dynamics of exercise adaptations from an integrated perspective. Cheng Karolinska Institutet COMMENTARY ON VIEWPOINT: THE RIGOROUS STUDY OF EXERCISE ADAPTATIONS: WHY mRNA MIGHT NOT BE ENOUGH TO THE EDITOR: The use of mRNA proﬁling is essential in bottom-up approaches for biological discovery. Miller et al.’s Viewpoint (1) is that “using mRNA outcomes in exercise studies provide limited insight into exercise adaptation” and “should be used as supportive rather than a primary out- come”(1). A few further considerations deserve mentioning to expand these views and maximize the usefulness of mRNA changes as a primary outcome when studying responses to acute exercise and adaptations to training. Delimitations and limitations in study design, technologies, and data analysis are major barriers for using mRNA changes as a primary outcome. Issues needed to be considered when undertaking transcrip- tome analysis include: 1) Study design: Changes in muscle mRNAs levels do not necessarily coincide with ongoing adap- tive responses (2, 4). Some mRNAs change before, whereas others change once the phenotypes manifest. Some mRNA responses are modiﬁed by training status or, depending on the transcripts, expression levels may coincide with the resulting phenotype (3). Thus, contingent on study design, time course, and training status, screening mRNA changes may/may not serve as good primary outcome. 2) Sensitivity: PCR vs. mi- croarrays vs. RNA Seq. Studies employing low resolution platforms (PCR, microarrays) offer limited possibilities to identify changes in mRNAs and other RNA species. Yet a focused analysis of mRNAs by using a PCR-based approach may yield signiﬁcant information about the behavior of speciﬁc mRNAs. Deep sequencing holds the promise to reveal sensi- tive gene expression patterns. Thus whether the choice of technology represents a limiting factor in transcriptome studies depends on the question being asked. 3) Noise and Analytics: Noise in gene expression is a stochastic phenomenon, and multicellularity in the tissue(s) sampled is a confounding vari- able that adds noise to gene expression proﬁles (5). Smart algorithms that reduce high “negative false discovery rates” common in stringent analytical approaches are necessary. Thus the robustness of the stimulus and analytical workﬂow em- ployed may overcome certain limitations in the identiﬁcation of regulatory gene networks controlling exercise-induced phe- notypes. Approach, study design, subject characteristics, and analytics condition the suitability of mRNA proﬁling as a primary outcome in exercise training studies. REFERENCES 1. Nader Pennsylvania State University EXERCISE ADAPTATIONS: THE WHOLE IS GREATER THAN THE SUM OF ITS PARTS TO THE EDITOR: The Molecular Transducers of Physical Activity Consortium will undoubtedly boost our understanding of the signaling pathways that underlie exercise-induced skeletal muscle adaptations. However, as Miller and colleagues (4) point out, “mRNA should be regarded as a supportive rather than a primary outcome.” In addition to their excellent account on signaling networks that govern exercise responses, we would like to emphasize the central role of physiological effects, particularly in mitochondria. Endurance exercise does not only regulate transcription and translation of nuclear DNA, but also mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) (2). The mitochondrial gene pool is evolutionary conserved and provides local production of proteins indispens- able for optimal mitochondrial respiration. Few studies have provided insight into the regulation of mtDNA transcription and translation, and the coordination with nuclear DNA-en- coded complexes after exercise (training). Moreover, mito- chondrial physiology strongly depends on its dynamics. Mito- chondria are not independent organelles, but form a reticulum that provides a conductive pathway for energy distribution (1). A fused connected reticulum occurs after exercise (5) or fasting (3). These changes occur as a rapid response to these chal- lenges and are primarily controlled by posttranscriptional pro- cesses. Finally, metabolic processes are at least partly regulated by substrate availability, and as such, metabolic ﬂuxes are difﬁcult to predict from mRNA or protein data. Understanding the signaling pathways that lead to an integrated response to exercise is highly valuable, but it seems that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. REFERENCES 1.
